title: III. The Self-Model: Identity as Reflexive Social Modeling
excerpt: The capacity to model other minds has a necessary reflexive consequence: an agent that can represent "what believes about the world" can also represent "what believes about me ." Once this representational capacity is in place, evolution can–and did–exploit it
html:
The capacity to model other minds has a necessary reflexive consequence: an agent that can represent "what jj believes about the world" can also represent "what jj believes about me." Once this representational capacity is in place, evolution can–and did–exploit it to construct a self-model: a generative model Pi(si,θi)P_i(s^i, \theta^i) of one’s own stable dispositions, values, social roles, competencies, and relational commitments that functions simultaneously as (a) a prior over one’s own future behavior (reducing planning costs by constraining the policy search space), (b) a prediction about how others will model oneself (enabling strategic self-presentation and reputation management), and (c) a social signal (communicating to others what kind of agent one is, thereby facilitating coordination and trust). What we call identity is, computationally, this self-model–and its maintenance, defense, and strategic deployment constitute a superordinate objective that pervades human cognition and motivation. A 2026 neuroimaging study compares self- and other-related mentalizing (Figure) 47. The authors test generalization to another social inference task (Figure).

Why Identity Coherence is Valuable

The value of maintaining a coherent self-model can be derived from all three superordinate objectives discussed previously:

Compression: A compact self-model dramatically reduces the computational cost of planning. Instead of evaluating the full policy space Π\Pi at every decision point, the agent can constrain search to the much smaller subset Πθi⊂Π\Pi_{\theta^i} \subset \Pi consistent with its self-model parameters ("I am the kind of person who does XX and does not do YY"). Internalized values, moral commitments, and role-based expectations function as learned priors over policy space P(π∣θi)P(\pi \mid \theta^i) that prune the decision tree before deliberation begins–yielding faster, less effortful, and more consistent action selection. In description-length terms, a coherent identity compresses behavioral history into a low-dimensional trait vector from which specific actions can be reconstructed (predicted), rather than requiring independent explanation for each choice.

Empowerment: A consistent, predictable identity is a prerequisite for sustained social empowerment. Other agents will cooperate with, invest in, and grant influence to ii only insofar as they can predict ii’s future behavior–and predictability requires that ii’s behavior be generated by stable parameters θi\theta^i rather than shifting capriciously. Trust, which is at root a confident prediction that the other will honor commitments, depends on the perceived stability and coherence of the partner’s self-model 1. An agent with an incoherent or rapidly shifting identity is a noisy channel from the perspective of social partners: their actions are unpredictable, their promises unreliable, and investment in them is high-risk. By maintaining identity coherence, the agent reduces H(Ssocial′∣Ai)H(S'_{\text{social}} \mid A_i) for social partners–making itself a reliable, decodable element in others’ generative models–and in return receives the cooperative benefits (trust, alliance, resources, status) that constitute social empowerment.

EFE risk minimization: Because social exclusion and reputational collapse are viability-level threats (see opening paragraphs), maintaining alignment between self-model and others’ models of self is directly risk-reducing. Large divergences between Pi(θi)P_i(\theta^i) ("who I think I am") and 𝔼j[Pj(θi)]\mathbb{E}_j[P_j(\theta^i)] ("who others think I am") create vulnerability: if the agent’s behavior suddenly deviates from what social partners expect, the resulting social prediction errors in others trigger suspicion, withdrawal, or punishment. Identity coherence minimizes the expected KL divergence 𝔼j[DKL[Pj(θi)∥Pi(θi)]]\mathbb{E}_j[D_{KL}[P_j(\theta^i) \| P_i(\theta^i)]] between self-model and others’ models, keeping the agent within the social viability manifold.

Identity as a Learned Constraint on the Preference Landscape

A critical insight is that identity does not merely describe the agent’s dispositions–it actively constrains them. Once a self-model Pi(θi)P_i(\theta^i) is established and socially communicated (through behavior, explicit declarations, group affiliation, and narrative), deviation from it becomes costly: internally through cognitive dissonance (aversive prediction error against the self-model), and externally through reputational damage (others’ models of ii are violated, triggering trust revision). These costs function as a regularizer on the policy space, penalizing actions that are inconsistent with stated/inferred identity even when those actions would be locally reward-maximizing. In EFE terms, identity commitments enter both P(oτ)P(o_\tau) (preferred outcomes include "behave consistently with my values") and P(π)P(\pi) (prior over policies concentrates mass on identity-consistent action plans), effectively converting a learned self-description into a normative constraint. This is the computational mechanism underlying the common observation that people will sacrifice material payoffs to maintain identity consistency–refusing to "sell out," honoring commitments at personal cost, punishing identity-inconsistent behavior in themselves and others–behaviors that are puzzling under narrow reward maximization but follow naturally from a system that treats self-model coherence as a high-weight objective.

Identity Threat and Defense

If the self-model functions as a high-precision prior, then evidence contradicting it will generate large prediction errors–and the system will be strongly motivated to minimize these errors, either by updating the model or by discounting / reinterpreting the evidence. In practice, because the self-model is both deeply entrenched (trained over a lifetime of behavioral evidence) and costly to revise (triggering downstream changes in social commitments, group memberships, and others’ models of self), the system is generally biased toward evidence discounting over model revision–the computational basis of ego-defense mechanisms. Cognitive dissonance 2 is the phenomenological signature of a large self-model prediction error: the aversive arousal generated when one’s behavior or outcomes contradict one’s self-model. The resolution strategies documented in the dissonance literature–rationalization, selective attention, post-hoc attitude change, trivialization of the inconsistency–are all instances of approximate posterior maintenance: adjusting auxiliary beliefs and interpretive frames to reduce the apparent prediction error without revising the core self-model parameters θi\theta^i, analogous to a generative model that explains away surprising observations through changes in context variables rather than deep structural revision. Self-serving attributional biases (attributing success to internal/stable factors and failure to external/unstable ones) serve the same function: they maintain the precision of the self-efficacy component of θi\theta^i by routing negative evidence away from the self-model. Self-affirmation effects–whereby reminding individuals of valued aspects of their identity buffers against threatening information in unrelated domains 3–are consistent with a system that evaluates threat relative to overall self-model coherence: bolstering one facet of the model increases the effective prior precision, rendering the system more tolerant of local prediction errors elsewhere. The study applies its classifiers to social feedback (Figure).

Neural Implementation and Architectural Priors

Cortical midline structures (CMS) as the self-model substrate. The neural substrate of the self-model is anchored in the cortical midline structures (CMS)–medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC, both ventromedial and dorsomedial), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and precuneus – regions that form the anterior and posterior hubs of the default mode network and show a reliable activation signature during self-referential processing across dozens of paradigms and meta-analyses 4, 5, 6. When subjects evaluate trait adjectives for self-relevance ("Am I honest?"), recall autobiographical memories, imagine their personal future, or reflect on their own preferences and attitudes, CMS activation consistently exceeds that observed during matched other-referential or semantic control conditions 7, 8. Within this system, a functional division is evident: The study tests multivariate brain signatures of mentalizing (Figure). The study also evaluates individual brain regions (Figure).

Ventromedial PFC (vmPFC): evaluative self-representation–integrating self-relevant information with affective value; vmPFC damage produces impaired social decision-making and flattened self-evaluation without loss of self-knowledge per se, consistent with a role in computing the "value of being me" rather than storing self-descriptive content 9, 10. vmPFC also supports the representation of personal values and moral identity 11, 12, positioning it as the locus where identity commitments interface with the valuation system. The valuation schematic relates self-relevance to prefrontal processing (Figure).

Dorsomedial PFC (dmPFC): reflective self-representation and explicit self-other comparison; dmPFC is engaged when subjects explicitly evaluate their own traits, compare self to others, or consider how they appear from a third-person perspective 8, 6. This is the region that most directly supports the reflexive function–modeling oneself-as-modeled-by-others–and it overlaps heavily with the mentalizing network (Section I), consistent with the claim that self-modeling is architecturally parasitic on other-modeling. The study compares self- and other-related activity (Figure).

Posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) / precuneus: autobiographical integration and self-continuity–providing the temporal "backbone" of the self-model by linking current self-representation to the remembered past and imagined future 13, 14. PCC shows the highest baseline metabolic rate of any cortical region and is a major DMN hub, reflecting its continuous role in maintaining the contextual frame ("who am I, where have I been, where am I going") against which current experience is interpreted.

The heavy overlap between the self-model system and the DMN is not incidental–it reflects the deep architectural relationship between identity and offline compression. The DMN’s core function, as discussed in the "Intrinsic Motivation" section, is generative simulation and schema extraction: converting episodic experience into compressed latent structure. The self-model is one such schema–the compressed representation that renders the agent’s own behavioral history predictable from a small number of trait parameters–and its construction and maintenance are core operations of the DMN’s offline consolidation engine. During rest, mind-wandering, and sleep, a substantial fraction of DMN activity is self-referential: spontaneous thought is disproportionately self-focused, autobiographical replay is biased toward identity-relevant episodes, and prospective simulation preferentially explores futures relevant to personal goals and social commitments 15, 16. This architecture means the self-model is continuously "retrained" offline, with priority given to experiences that update trait-level self-knowledge–explaining why identity-threatening events (social humiliation, moral failures, achievements that exceed expectation) produce intense offline rumination (high-salience training data demanding model revision) and why disruption of DMN consolidation (sleep deprivation, chronic stress) can destabilize the self-model.

Hippocampal–mPFC circuits: autobiographical memory as the evidence base. The self-model is not built from current sensory input but from the accumulated autobiographical evidence base: the corpus of remembered episodes that, once compressed, yields the trait-level parameters θi\theta^i. The hippocampus provides the episodic component–encoding specific events with their spatiotemporal and affective context–while mPFC extracts the invariants across episodes that constitute stable self-knowledge 17, 18. This division mirrors the CLS framework (Section on the DMN): hippocampus as fast, high-fidelity store; cortex (including mPFC) as slow, compressed, schema-level store. A critical implication is that autobiographical memory is not a neutral recording system but a self-model-maintaining reconstruction engine: memories are recalled not veridically but in a manner biased toward consistency with the current self-model 19, 20. Memory distortion in the service of identity coherence–remembering oneself as more consistent, more virtuous, more competent than the raw data would support–is not a "bug" but a feature of a system whose primary objective is to maintain a low-complexity, high-predictive-accuracy self-model that supports effective social functioning. The well-documented reminiscence bump (disproportionate recall of events from adolescence and early adulthood 21) is consistent with this framework: the self-model’s foundational parameters are installed during the identity-formation period (see developmental trajectory below), and episodes from this critical window receive priority encoding and retention because they contributed most to defining θi\theta^i.

Insular cortex: the interoceptive self. The self-model is not exclusively a cognitive/narrative construction–it includes a somatic component representing "how I characteristically feel." The anterior insula, as the cortical terminus of interoceptive processing, maintains a representation of current and predicted body states that contributes to the subjective sense of self as an embodied, feeling agent. Individual differences in interoceptive accuracy (the ability to accurately detect one’s own heartbeat, respiration, etc.) correlate with the stability and clarity of self-concept 22, 23, consistent with the idea that the self-model is anchored in interoceptive prediction as well as social/narrative construction. Disruption of insular processing (as in depersonalization/derealization disorder) produces the phenomenological experience of estrangement from one’s own body and identity–a self-model prediction error at the somatic level that the system cannot resolve 24.

Right-lateralized fronto-parietal circuits: body ownership and self-other boundary. At the most basic sensorimotor level, the self-model must specify which body belongs to "me" and which sensory events are self-caused versus externally generated. Right-lateralized fronto-parietal regions–including right TPJ, right inferior parietal lobule, right premotor cortex, and right insula–support this bodily self-model by integrating multisensory signals (visual, proprioceptive, vestibular, interoceptive) into a coherent estimate of body ownership and agency 25, 26. The rubber hand illusion (in which synchronous visuotactile stimulation shifts perceived hand ownership to a prosthetic hand 27) and full-body illusions (in which vestibular-visual conflict produces out-of-body experience phenomenology 28) demonstrate that body ownership is inferred from multisensory evidence rather than given a priori–it is a posterior estimate that can be manipulated by altering the likelihood model. This bodily self-model provides the foundation layer of identity: before there can be a narrative self ("I am a kind person") or social self ("I am a member of group GG"), there must be an embodied self ("this body is mine and these actions are mine"), and this foundation is constructed from phylogenetically ancient multisensory integration circuits that are already functional at birth, albeit imprecisely calibrated.

Social Identity and Group-Level Self-Models

In humans, the self-model extends beyond individual traits and dispositions to include group memberships as core identity components. Social identity theory 29 and self-categorization theory 30 document that categorizing oneself as a member of a group ("I am a [member of GG]") triggers a suite of automatic consequences: activation of group-prototypical norms as behavioral priors, favoritism toward in-group members, derogation or homogenization of out-group members, and willingness to sacrifice personal interests for group welfare. From a computational perspective, social identity functions as a hierarchical extension of the self-model: when GG-membership is activated, the agent’s policy priors shift from purely individual parameters P(π∣θi)P(\pi \mid \theta^i) to group-level parameters P(π∣θG)P(\pi \mid \theta^G), importing the group’s norms, values, and behavioral expectations as constraints on one’s own action selection. This is a powerful compression heuristic in social environments: rather than learning an individual policy for every social context, the agent can index into group-level policies that encode the accumulated cultural knowledge of GG about appropriate behavior in context CC. In-group favoritism and out-group homogeneity bias are explained within this framework as a model-selection economy: in-group members are modeled using the shared θG\theta^G prior (cheap, often accurate given genuine within-group similarity in norms and values), while out-group members are modeled using a coarser, less differentiated prior (fewer training episodes, lower motivation to invest in individual-level modeling) 31.

The minimal group paradigm 32–in which mere arbitrary categorization (e.g., preference for Klee vs. Kandinsky paintings) is sufficient to produce in-group favoritism and out-group discrimination–demonstrates how readily the social identity system can be activated, suggesting low thresholds and strong default priors. The neural correlates include: differential mPFC activation when processing in-group vs. out-group targets (more individuated, self-like processing for in-group 8, 33); ventral striatum activation for in-group reward and cooperation (in-group coordination is intrinsically rewarding 34); amygdala response modulation by racial and group-category cues (with magnitude influenced by implicit bias and modulated by individuation goals 35, 36); and ACC/AI activation when observing in-group members’ suffering (empathic resonance is amplified for in-group, attenuated for out-group, absent deliberate regulatory effort 37, 38). This in-group empathy bias is a direct consequence of the simulation route’s egocentric default: in-group members are perceived as more "like me," hence the self-model is a better proxy, and simulation is more readily engaged. The brain-response comparison illustrates identity-dependent social valuation (Figure).

The evolutionary basis for social identity is likely rooted in coalitional psychology: across the hominin lineage, between-group competition created intense selection pressure for mechanisms that facilitate rapid coalition detection, in-group coordination, and out-group vigilance 39, 40. The ease with which social identity biases are activated (minimal groups), their early developmental onset (in-group preference by ∼\sim5 years [The development of implicit intergroup

cognition]), and their cross-cultural ubiquity suggest that the architecture for group-based self-categorization is genetically specified–evolution installed a "group membership slot" in the self-model that is ready to be filled by whatever cultural group structure the developing child encounters. The content (which groups, which norms, which boundaries) is learned, but the capacity to define oneself in terms of group membership and to automatically activate group-level behavioral priors upon categorization is an architectural prior.

Developmental Trajectory

The self-model develops through a sequence that recapitulates the layered architecture, with each level depending on the maturation of its neural substrate:

Bodily self (0-18 months): Multisensory self–other discrimination, sense of agency over motor outputs, proprioceptive body schema. Supported by early-maturing right-lateralized fronto-parietal circuits and somatosensory cortex. The mirror self-recognition milestone (∼\sim18 months 41) marks the point at which the visual body image is integrated into the self-model with sufficient coherence to support recognition of one’s own reflection.

Categorical/objective self (18 months - 3 years): Emergence of self-referential language ("I," "me," "mine"), self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, shame–requiring a model of how others evaluate the self 42), and early self-description in terms of observable attributes (age, gender, physical features). This stage depends on the development of representational capacity in mPFC and temporal-pole person-knowledge circuits, and on the linguistic tools that enable self-referential encoding.

Narrative/trait self (middle childhood): Self-description shifts from concrete attributes to psychological traits ("I am shy," "I am good at math"), reflecting the abstraction of behavioral regularities into stable dispositional parameters θi\theta^i 43. This development tracks the maturation of dmPFC trait-inference circuitry and the expansion of autobiographical memory networks (hippocampal-mPFC consolidation of self-relevant episodes into schematic self-knowledge).

Identity exploration and commitment (adolescence): The self-model undergoes its most substantial reorganization, driven by the convergence of (i) prefrontal maturation (synaptic pruning and myelination in mPFC and frontopolar cortex, enabling more abstract and temporally extended self-representation 44), (ii) pubertal neuroendocrine changes (gonadal hormones reorganize social-motivational circuits, shifting reward sensitivity toward peer approval and status 45), and (iii) social-ecological transition (expanded peer networks, reduced parental supervision, identity-relevant choices about education, values, and group affiliation). Erikson’s identity crisis 46 corresponds, in this framework, to a period of high-variance, high-learning-rate exploration over self-model parameter space: the system temporarily relaxes the coherence prior to test alternative identity configurations before committing to a stable adult θi\theta^i. Heightened adolescent sensitivity to social evaluation, self-consciousness, and peer influence reflects the increased precision weighting on social feedback signals during this calibration period–exactly what an optimal meta-learning system would do when the self-model is undergoing substantial revision and external validation is informative. The study examines self–other discrimination across adolescence (Figure). A 2026 study tests adolescent responses to online social feedback (Figure) 48. The study compares feedback conditions (Figure). The study also records event-related EEG responses (Figure).

Adult identity maintenance and revision: The mature self-model operates with a relatively high-precision prior over θi\theta^i, supporting rapid and consistent action selection but resisting revision. The self-model is continuously but slowly updated by ongoing experience (career outcomes, relationship feedback, aging, life transitions), with major revisions occurring during identity-disrupting life events (divorce, bereavement, job loss, religious conversion, immigration) that generate self-model prediction errors large enough to overcome the coherence prior. The balance between stability and plasticity is modulated by the same neuromodulatory systems that govern learning rate elsewhere: noradrenergic signals that detect "regime change" can transiently increase the self-model’s learning rate, enabling faster identity revision when circumstances demand it, while serotonergic and oxytocinergic modulation of social confidence and relational security influence the baseline precision of the trait-level prior (see Sections IV and V).

In sum, the self-model system is built on: (i) CMS architecture – phylogenetically conserved midline cortical structures (with homologues across mammals) genetically wired to integrate multimodal evidence about the organism’s own states, traits, and values; (ii) DMN connectivity – long-range white-matter connections linking anterior (mPFC) and posterior (PCC/precuneus) midline hubs with hippocampal memory systems and lateral temporal person-knowledge stores, establishing the network topology for self-referential processing before experiential content is available; (iii) right-lateralized multisensory integration circuits for the bodily self-model, providing the foundational layer of self–other distinction; (iv) a social identity slot – the coalitional-psychology architecture that allows group memberships to function as identity components, modulating empathy, norm compliance, and intergroup behavior; and (v) a rostro-caudal developmental gradient in which the self-model is built bottom-up across ontogeny (bodily self →\rightarrow categorical self →\rightarrow trait self →\rightarrow narrative/ideological identity), with each layer depending on the maturation schedule of its prefrontal substrate and the availability of appropriate social training data. Evolution does not install a specific identity – it installs the representational architecture and developmental program that guarantees a self-model will be constructed from the organism’s particular social embedding, and that once constructed, it will function as a high-inertia prior that simultaneously compresses one’s own behavioral complexity, signals reliability to social partners, and constrains future policy in identity-consistent (and therefore socially predictable) directions.
